title: Operative reduction of intussusception
subtitle: Squeeze, do not pull; resect when it will not reduce or is not viable

sources.title: Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: intussusception
Operative Pediatric Surgery (Spitz L, Coran AG, editors): intussusception

indications: Failed or incomplete radiological (air or hydrostatic) enema reduction, after any repeat attempt the radiologist and surgeon agree is safe.
Peritonitis, perforation, or shock that does not respond to resuscitation, in which enema reduction is contraindicated.
A pathological lead point seen on imaging or suspected because of age or recurrence.
Persistent, symptomatic small bowel to small bowel intussusception that does not resolve.
contraindications: Transient small bowel intussusception found on ultrasound in a well child: usually resolves and is observed.
An unresuscitated child: resuscitation comes first, but it is a reason to optimise, not to delay indefinitely.
A laparoscopic approach may be used by experienced surgeons in a stable child without peritonitis; convert to open when reduction fails.
preparation: Review the enema report: number of attempts, how far reduction progressed, and any perforation.
Fluid resuscitation, nasogastric tube, bloods with group and crossmatch, and antibiotics if perforation or peritonitis is suspected.
Consent the parents for: bowel resection with anastomosis, a stoma (rare), wound infection, adhesive obstruction later, recurrence, anastomotic leak, and appendicectomy at the same operation.
positioning: Supine on a warmed mattress, with the abdomen fully exposed and a roll under the lower chest if needed.
equipment: Paediatric laparotomy set, warm moist packs, bipolar diathermy.
Fine absorbable monofilament sutures for a handsewn anastomosis.
Laparoscopic set if that approach is chosen.
anatomy: Most childhood intussusceptions are ileocolic: the terminal ileum (intussusceptum) telescopes into the colon (intussuscipiens), drawing its mesentery with it.
The mesentery is compressed within the intussusception, producing venous congestion, oedema, then arterial ischaemia of the intussusceptum.
The apex may reach anywhere along the colon, occasionally to the rectum.
Hypertrophied Peyer patches in the terminal ileum are the usual lead point in idiopathic cases and feel like a mass after reduction; they are not an indication for resection.
Pathological lead points include Meckel diverticulum, polyps, duplication cysts, lymphoma and submucosal haematoma in IgA vasculitis.
criticalSafety: Reduce by squeezing the apex back from distal to proximal; never pull the proximal bowel out of the intussuscipiens.
Assess viability after reduction with warm packs and time, not in the first minute.
Feel for a pathological lead point after every reduction.
structuresAtRisk: Oedematous bowel wall, which splits under traction
Caecal wall at the appendix base
commonErrors: Pulling on the ileum to reduce the last part, causing a serosal tear or perforation.
Abandoning reduction too early at the ileocaecal valve, where the final part is always slowest.
Resecting a thickened Peyer patch mistaken for a tumour.
Missing a Meckel diverticulum lead point because the bowel was not run after reduction.
complications: Recurrent intussusception, less common after operative reduction than after enema reduction.
Adhesive small bowel obstruction later in life.
postop: Intravenous fluids and nasogastric drainage until the ileus settles, then feeding as tolerated.
Weight-based analgesia; continue antibiotics only where there was perforation or resection, per local policy.
Chase histology for any resected specimen, and explain to the parents what was found and the small risk of recurrence.

steps.emphasis: Consent covers resection, stoma and appendicectomy, so no decision in theatre needs a second conversation.
State the enema result, whether perforation occurred, and blood availability.
Treat as contaminated surgery if perforation is suspected; agent per local policy.
Prepare the whole abdomen: the apex may be in the left colon.
Right-sided transverse incision, placed over the mass felt under anaesthesia.
Wrap the reduced bowel in warm moist packs and wait several minutes. Look for colour, peristalsis and mesenteric pulsation; multiple or deep serosal splits count against viability.
Only after resection: single-layer extramucosal ileocolic anastomosis with fine monofilament, correcting the calibre mismatch on the ileal side.
Any resected segment goes for histology with the question of a lead point stated.
Record how far the intussusception reached, whether manual reduction was complete, viability, any lead point and whether the appendix was removed.

step.intus.deliver.title: Finding and delivering the intussusception
step.intus.deliver.why: Reduction is safest when it is done under direct vision with the bowel outside the wound. Bowel reduced by blind pressure inside the abdomen cannot be watched for splitting.
how: Follow the colon from the caecal area to find the apex of the mass, which may lie anywhere from the right colon to the pelvis.
Deliver the mass and the adjacent bowel into the wound, mobilising the right colon if needed to bring it up without traction.
Note any free fluid, perforation or obviously gangrenous bowel before handling it further.
pitfalls: Lifting the mass out by pulling on the ileum.
Forcing a large mass through a small incision instead of extending it.

step.intus.reduce.title: Manual reduction by retrograde squeezing
step.intus.reduce.why: Pushing the apex back from below spreads force over the whole wall. Pulling on the proximal bowel concentrates it at the neck, where the oedematous wall splits and perforates.
how: Hold the colon just distal to the apex and squeeze the apex gently backwards towards the caecum, like expressing a tube from its far end.
Keep steady, patient pressure; the last part through the ileocaecal valve is always the slowest and oedema yields with time.
Use warm moist packs and gentle sustained compression of the oedematous ileum to reduce swelling before continuing.
Stop if the serosa begins to split in several places or the bowel will not move after patient effort: proceed to resection.
pitfalls: A final tug on the ileum to finish the reduction.
Repeated forceful attempts on an obviously gangrenous segment.

step.intus.lead-point.title: Searching for a pathological lead point
step.intus.lead-point.why: A missed lead point means recurrence or a missed diagnosis such as lymphoma. Lead points are more likely outside the usual age range for idiopathic intussusception and in recurrent cases.
how: After reduction, palpate the terminal ileum, caecum and colon for a discrete intraluminal mass.
Distinguish the soft, thickened Peyer patch of idiopathic intussusception from a firm discrete lesion.
Run the small bowel from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal valve, specifically looking for a Meckel diverticulum or a duplication.
If a lead point is found, resect it with the involved segment.
pitfalls: Resecting a Peyer patch as a tumour.
Not running the small bowel because the obvious problem has been reduced.

step.intus.resect.title: Resection when reduction fails or the bowel is not viable
step.intus.resect.why: An irreducible, perforated or gangrenous intussusception, or one with a lead point, needs resection. A limited resection with primary anastomosis is usually safe in a resuscitated child; a stoma is the choice when the child or the field is not.
how: Resect the involved segment, usually as a limited ileocolic resection, dividing the mesentery close to the bowel since this is a benign resection unless a tumour is suspected.
Restore continuity with a primary handsewn anastomosis when the child is stable and the ends are healthy.
Bring out a stoma instead when the child is unstable, contamination is gross, or perfusion of the ends is doubtful, and inform the consultant.
structuresAtRisk: Mesentery of the retained ileum and colon
pitfalls: An anastomosis on ends of doubtful perfusion in a septic child.
An extended oncological resection for what is a Peyer patch.
